836 PM EDT Tue Oct 6 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
With the National Hurricane Center upgrading the tropical invest
to Tropical Depression #9, have adjusted the wording accordingly
in Key Message 2.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Quiet weather conditions are expected through the end of
     the week.

- 2) Increased rain potential late this weekend into early next
     week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Quiet weather conditions are expected through
the end of the week.

High pressure will shift offshore tonight allowing for a
slightly warmer night as winds become slightly elevated. 
However, many locations will still be in the lower to mid 40s, 
with some upper 30s possible in the more sheltered valleys given
the dry nature of the air mass. Given the cool temperatures, 
some patchy river valley fog is possible, especially west of the
Blue Ridge. Winds turn southerly Wednesday allowing temps to 
climb back into the 70s. Temperatures warm up to near 80 
Thursday before the passage of another dry cold front. Temps 
cool off slightly for the end of the week as weak high pressure 
of Canadian origin builds in. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Increased rain potential late this weekend into
early next week. 

The National Hurricane Center is currently monitoring a disturbance 
over the southwestern Gulf of America (TD 9). It is anticipated
that moisture associated with what is now TD 9 will move into 
our region later this weekend or early next week. There are a 
lot of possibilities for where this system goes, and by 
extension, the potential impacts that could bring to our area. 
There will be a few key features ahead of this system to watch, 
but the most important will be a cutoff low expected to develop 
over TX. Cutoff lows are notoriously difficult to forecast, 
hence, the level of uncertainty with the forecast. At this 
juncture, several scenarios appear possible:

(1) Quick-moving low pressure moves onshore of the Gulf Coast, and 
threads the needle between high pressure over the Southwest Atlantic 
and the Upper Midwest, allowing it to move further north toward the 
OH Valley, central Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic, delivering notably 
higher rain potential and amounts locally.

(2) A very quick-moving low pressure system is forced to make an 
eastward turn sooner across the Southeast prior to the western 
extent of SW Atlantic ridging exiting the coast. This would keep a 
majority of moisture and rain chances to our south, though some 
moisture could still be drawn northward along a passing front.

(3) A slow-moving low pressure system is forced to make that 
eastward turn sooner, blocked in this scenario by the second area of 
high pressure in the Upper Midwest building in before it can trek 
too far to the north. This would keep nearly all precipitation and 
moisture associated with the low suppressed to the south.

(4) A very slow-moving area of low pressure would not only get 
caught beneath ridging building over the Upper Midwest, but could 
then remain cutoff from the large scale steering pattern. This would 
leave low pressure meandering somewhere well to our south for a 
time, before an uncertain exit beyond the current forecast period.

At the moment, deterministic and ensemble medium range guidance 
exhibits very large spread, falling into (but not necessarily 
favoring) any one of the four scenarios listed above.

It will be important to stay tuned to the forecast over the next few 
days, and monitor hurricanes.gov for details on any potential 
further development of TD 9.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
VFR conditions are expected through the end of the week. Winds
turn southerly Wednesday as high pressure shifts offshore. A dry
cold front Thu will cause another wind shift to the west and
northwest into Fri.

VFR conditions are expected on Friday and Saturday as high pressure 
remains dominant over the region. Winds will be out of the N or 
NW on Friday at around 5 to 10 knots, before switching out of 
the S to SE on Saturday at the same speed. 

More uncertainty going into Sunday, but sub-VFR conditions are 
possible if we do manage to get any rain associated with the area of 
low pressure over the southwestern Gulf of America.

&&

.MARINE...
Winds are expected to strengthen Wednesday out of the south and
could flirt with marginal SCA conditions Wednesday evening. A
dry frontal passage Thursday could bring another period of
marginal SCA conditions Thursday afternoon into Thursday night.

Winds are expected to remain below SCA criteria on Friday and 
Saturday as high pressure remains dominant over the region. However, 
by Saturday evening, we could see a brief burst of southerly 
channeling winds that come close to criteria. Confidence is low at 
this time.
